title: Woman, 87, dies after being carried from home of 70 years on stretcher during eviction in Spain
summary: Maricarmen Abascal's eviction from her Madrid apartment of 70 years sparked massive protests, and her death has deepened Spain's housing crisis.
story: Fox News contributor Jason Chaffetz discusses the Democratic Socialists of America platform and draws parallels between its policies and Spain's ongoing migration crisis.

The death of an 87-year-old woman who was evicted from her longtime home has intensified a political crisis in Spain, where nationwide protests over soaring housing costs have helped force an early election.

María del Carmen Abascal, known as "Maricarmen," died Wednesday after being hospitalized following her eviction from a Madrid apartment where she had lived for seven decades, according to The Associated Press.
Her death came just days after Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for Nov. 29 after his government's failure to pass emergency housing measures through Parliament.
The controversy has put renewed pressure on Sánchez's Socialist Party as Spain grapples with widespread frustration over rising rents and housing affordability.
SPANISH OPPOSITION LEADER CALLS PRIME MINISTER A ‘TRAITOR’ OVER CEUTA MIGRANT CRISIS
People rally in downtown Madrid, Spain, to honor the memory of Maria del Carmen Abascal, 87, whose eviction from her home sparked nationwide protests Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)

At the center of the uproar was Abascal's Sept. 23 eviction, which drew national attention after images showed the elderly woman, who used a wheelchair, being carried from her apartment on a stretcher.
Police had cordoned off the street and removed demonstrators who attempted to stop the eviction.
The images sparked demonstrations in Madrid and other Spanish cities, turning Abascal into a symbol of the country's housing crisis.
The real estate company responsible for her eviction had sought to lease the apartment at a substantially higher price, according to the AP.
ANGRY LOCALS BLOCK FAMOUS BEACH AS MASS TOURISM PROTESTS ESCALATE AT VACATION HOT SPOT

A view of the door of the home from which Maria del Carmen Abascal, 87, was evicted, sparking nationwide protests, with a sign reading "Rest in peace, Maricarmen," in Madrid, Spain, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026 (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)
Facing mounting public pressure, the company eventually agreed to allow Abascal to return to her home. She died before she could move back.
Her cause of death has not been disclosed.
After news of her death, demonstrators gathered outside Spain's Parliament and in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square, where some observed a minute of silence.
Protesters also chanted, "Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!"
TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS

A woman places flowers in Madrid, Spain, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, near the entrance to the building where Maria del Carmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from her home, sparking nationwide protests. (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)
Sánchez offered condolences in a statement on X.
"All my love to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," he wrote. "A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace."
Conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also expressed condolences and urged political leaders not to use the woman's death for political gain.
"No campaign, no party, no use for political advantage," he wrote. "When faced with the death of a person, we must only show respect."
Abascal's eviction and death have become a rallying point for housing activists demanding changes to Spain's rental policies as the country prepares for its November election.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Iranian protester hanged hours after marrying his imprisoned fiancée over jail phone line
summary: Alireza Sepahi married his imprisoned fiancée over a prison phone line hours before his execution at Isfahan Central Prison for anti-government protest.
story: Iranian activist Sheyda Rahbari details the surge in executions of political dissidents by the terrorist Islamic regime. She notes the regime's increasing pressure on its people, openly threatening them with arrest and execution. Rahbari cites the execution of an 18-year-old protestor, Amir Hussein Hamedi, as a heartbreaking example of the regime's brutality.
An Iranian anti-regime protester was hanged at dawn Oct. 5 inside Isfahan Central Prison, just hours after marrying his imprisoned fiancée over a jail phone line, The Times reported Thursday.

Alireza Sepahi, 25, was executed alongside co-defendant Alireza Raisi after being sentenced to death in the anti-government demonstrations at Isfahan’s Alikhani Square Jan. 8., according to Human Rights Iran.
Sepahi and his bride, student activist Mahshad Keshani, 22, knew and loved each other before being arrested during anti-regime demonstrations, the report said.
IRAN HANGS 2 PROTESTERS IN PUBLIC, CROWD CRIES 'DISHONORABLE' AS SECURITY FIRES TEAR GAS
Alireza Sepahi, 25, was executed alongside co-defendant Alireza Raisi after being sentenced to death in the anti-government demonstrations at Isfahan’s Alikhani Square. (Iran Human Rights)
Keshani, who is serving a five-year sentence, pushed for an informal wedding Sunday as fears mounted that Sepahi’s execution was imminent after a final family summons.
The couple exchanged vows over the phone from inside Isfahan prison, joined by their fathers.
Human rights lawyer Amirsalar Davoudi facilitated the ceremony by reading the vows for the fathers to bless.
Keshani’s family gave a copy of the Quran, a saffron rock candy and a single red rose as a traditional dowry.
"It was Mahshad’s idea," Davoudi told The Times. "Even now, I wonder how one young woman can possess such courage."
IRAN TO EXECUTE FIRST FEMALE PROTESTER TIED TO ANTI-REGIME UNREST
Iranians attend an anti-government protest in Tehran, Iran, Jan. 9, 2026. (UGC via AP)
Davoudi recalled warning Keshani about the permanent nature of the decision.
"I told her, ‘My dear, you understand that this cannot simply be undone?’" Davoudi said.
"She said, ‘Mr Davoudi, I love Alireza.’"
When Davoudi presented the proposal to Sepahi, the young man broke down in tears.
"Alireza was crying, and something deeply painful and beautiful happened. Even the prison officers began to cry," Davoudi said.

The ceremony held no formal authority to halt the execution. Sepahi had previously survived a scheduled hanging in July after suffering a heart attack on his way to the gallows. Authorities then rescheduled the execution after he regained consciousness.
On Monday morning, hours after the vows were spoken, Sepahi was hanged.
IRAN'S REGIME CAME FOR TEENAGE TWINS. THEIR FATE OFFERS A GLIMPSE OF TEHRAN'S WIDENING DEATH CAMPAIGN
Iranian security forces escalated from pellet guns to live ammunition during protests. (Getty)
He is among seven defendants executed in the Alikhani Square case, in which 12 men were accused in the deaths of four security personnel.
After the hanging, Sepahi’s family was reportedly prevented by authorities from burying their son in his hometown.
Davoudi condemned the Iranian regime's actions.
"I do not know how to come to terms with this," Davoudi said.
"The regime is taking revenge on innocent young people for the humiliation it has suffered internationally."
Human rights groups report Keshani remains in custody, facing additional security charges.

This came as Maryam Rajavi, president-elect of the National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI), urged U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres to take immediate international action to halt executions and the killing of protesters in Iran, citing thousands of executions and decades of impunity for human rights abuses.

In a letter ahead of World Day Against the Death Penalty on Oct. 10, Rajavi called for international accountability, independent investigations and diplomatic and economic pressure on Tehran to end the executions.

title: Mother of dead Russian anti-plague institute worker: 'I know the truth'
summary: Svetlana Shipilova, the mother of the anti-plague institute worker who died in Russia, has reportedly spoken out following her daughter's death.
story: Fox News contributor Dr. Jessica Gray joins 'Fox & Friends First' to break down the transmission of the pneumonic plague, potential treatment options and the global health security risks. Experts emphasize the importance of early detection and international monitoring.

The mother of Darya Shipilova, the 28-year-old Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East worker whose death has sparked global public health concerns, pushed back against reports her daughter was infected after she broke a test tube.
Svetlana Shipilova, who is a medical professional, told the Russian outlet Glubina she does not believe the account circulating regarding her daughter's demise, according to The Telegraph.
"I know the truth," she reportedly said. "I’m having to fend off stupid acquaintances who believed all this. The clever ones didn’t believe it, of course.
RUSSIAN BIO-LEAK SECRECY FOLLOWS CHERNOBYL PLAYBOOK, EX-CIA OFFICER WARNS

Darya Shipilova, 28, an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died after developing pneumonia of an unknown cause, prompting quarantines and heightened health precautions in the region. Russian authorities say testing has found no evidence her illness was linked to pathogens she worked with. (East2West news)
"Not even all medical professionals understand it’s impossible to break a test tube like that," she added. "Even if you fling it at the wall. Only an amateur could say something like that.
"Even hypothetically, you simply can’t spill what’s inside or break the tube. They’re that well protected."
She also asserted to reporters, "They simply let my daughter die."
TRUMP RESPONDS TO CONCERNS OVER SUSPECTED PLAGUE CASE IN RUSSIA, SAYING US 'WILLING TO HELP'

World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus speaks on stage during World Forum 2026 on the "Future of Democracy, AI/Tech, and Humankind" as part of the Cinema for Peace events in Berlin Feb. 16, 2026. (Adam Berry/AFP via Getty Images)

Russian authorities have kept a tight lid on information about the case, saying only that the woman contracted pneumonia of "unknown" origin and that her tests were negative for the pathogens she worked with.

World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus noted during remarks Wednesday that "we don’t yet have the full picture of this event, and we are not able to conduct a full risk assessment."
RUSSIAN RESEARCHER'S MYSTERY DEATH COULD BE 'FAR WORSE' THAN THE PLAGUE, FORMER SENIOR TRUMP OFFICIAL WARNS
A view of the entrance to the grounds of the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk Oct. 7, 2026. (Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP via Getty Images)

"CDC is aware of and closely monitoring reports of a suspected case of pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region of Russia that resulted in a death," the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in part of a post Tuesday on X.
"We are working across the U.S. government to assess developments as additional information becomes available."

title: Teen wearing helmet camera kills worker at Polish school amid fears of copycat attacks
summary: A 15-year-old wearing a helmet camera allegedly killed a school employee and wounded two others in Poland's second school stabbing attack in two days.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A 15-year-old boy wielding a knife and wearing a helmet-mounted camera attacked a Polish primary school he used to attend, allegedly killing one employee and wounding two others in the country's second school stabbing in two days.
Authorities are investigating whether the attacks are connected to an online challenge encouraging teenagers to kill as many people as possible.
Police said a 37-year-old woman who worked as a caretaker died in the Thursday morning attack at the school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw.
The school's head teacher, Krzysztof Ochmanski, was injured while subduing the teenager, officials said. Ochmanski told a radio station he heard a scream and ran into a hallway.
Forensic investigators probe a knife attack at a vocational school in the town of Ostroleka, Poland, Oct. 7, 2026. (Mladen Antonov/AFP via Getty Images)
MOTHER ACCUSED OF TRYING TO KILL DAUGHTERS IN FREEWAY CRASH AND KNIFE ATTACK AS SOLDIERS STEP IN

"He wounded me with the blade of a rather long knife — he had three knives on him — and hit me with the handle," Ochmanski told the public broadcaster Polskie Radio RDC. "By then, I had managed to restrain him."
The day before the latest attack, a 19-year-old allegedly wounded 10 people, including himself, at a school in Ostroleka, which is in northeastern Poland.
Also this week, police arrested a 17-year-old in Sierpc in north-central Poland after authorities suspected he was planning a similar attack, Reuters reported.
Members of the media work next to an ambulance parked at the site of a knife attack at a vocational school in Ostroleka Oct. 7, 2026. (Mladen Antonov/AFP via Getty Images)
AMERICAN YOUTH RADICALIZED ONLINE, BUSTED IN SUSPECTED TERROR PLOTS AFTER HATING COUNTRY ON SOCIAL MEDIA

"We fear a grim copycat phenomenon," Prime Minister Donald Tusk told an emergency meeting, according to Reuters. "We are facing an extraordinary situation. ... For the first time, we are dealing with a killer who wore a helmet-mounted camera, intending to film the knife attack."
Tusk ordered police to visit schools every day to discourage further violence.
Children look at the scene of a knife attack at a vocational school in the town of Ostroleka Oct. 7, 2026. (Mladen Antonov/AFP via Getty Images)

Nikola, the 18-year-old sister of a boy at the school that was attacked Thursday, told Reuters there were rumors about the social media challenge that the police are now investigating.

"I mean, I didn't know if it was even real — I still don't know if it's true, actually — because it sounds so unreal, so terrifying, just like something out of a movie: some kind of challenge to kill as many people as possible," she said.

title: 'The world is standing with you': Christian leaders from 122 countries unite in Jerusalem for Oct 7
summary: The Friends of Zion summit drew delegations from 122 countries to Jerusalem, where released hostages and bereaved families shared their stories.
story: Buzolic, a devout Christian, was in Israel, where he hosted the Oct. 7 event of the Friends of Zion Ambassador's Summit in Jerusalem.
Christian community leaders and influencers from around the world gathered in Jerusalem Wednesday for an international memorial marking Oct. 7 as part of the Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit.

The event also included Jewish leaders, released hostages, bereaved families, wounded Israelis, ambassadors and diplomatic representatives to commemorate the anniversary of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, massacre.
"Oct. 7 is the worst day in Israel’s history, a day of hopelessness," Dr. Mike Evans, founder of the Friends of Zion Heritage Center in Jerusalem, told Fox News Digital.
ON OCT 7, CHRISTIANS MUST REMEMBER AND STAND WITH ISRAEL
Christian community leaders and influencers gathered in Jerusalem to commemorate the anniversary of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, massacre. (Hooman Khalili)

"People talk a lot about the more than 1,200 people killed that day, but not enough about the more than 70,000 who lost their homes and loved ones. You have a nation going through unspeakable pain, not only because of Oct. 7, but also because of the feeling that they are alone and that the world has turned against them," Evans added.

"What I’m sharing on Oct. 7 is this: ‘You’re wrong. The world is standing with you,’" he continued. "You see the faces, languages and songs of people from around the world united to comfort you and stand with you. It’s not political. It’s for the Jewish people: You are not alone. We’re with you. We love you."
CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND

Former hostages Evyatar David (far left), Agam Berger (center left), Sagui Dekel-Chen (center right) and Bar Kupershtein attend the Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit’s Oct. 7 international memorial event in Jerusalem Oct 7, 2026. (Friends of Zion)
Hosted by actor and influencer Nathaniel Buzolic and reporter Erin Molan, Wednesday’s event in the Israeli capital was broadcast live on dozens of television networks around the world.

"When other minority or groups suffer, there tends to be some sort of acknowledgment of that suffering, but when it comes to Jewish suffering, particularly at the hands of radical Islamists, there is not only silence but also denial and an attempt to downgrade the atrocities we witnessed, and we really have witnessed atrocities not just on Oct. 7 but in the continuation of that," Buzolic told Fox News Digital.

Buzolic said supporting Israel is a moral imperative given what he described as efforts to destroy the country. He argued that the hostility toward Israel is rooted in a radical Islamist ideology that rejects peace and coexistence not only with the Jewish state, but also with Western societies more broadly.

Released hostages Agam Berger, Sagui Dekel-Chen, Bar Kupershtein and Evyatar David attended the event, along with Bar’s grandfather, Holocaust survivor Michael Kupershtein. Sylvan Adams, president of the World Jewish Congress Israel and a full partner in the event, also participated.
ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS
Memorials at the site of the Oct. 7 Hamas terror attack on the Supernova music festival near Kibbutz Re'im, Israel, May 27, 2024. (Kobi Wolf/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Earlier in the day, participants visited Yad Vashem, Israel’s Holocaust remembrance center.
The Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit is being held for the second consecutive year and brings together over 1,000 participants from 122 countries.

"The alliance is very strong. The vast majority of Zionists in the world are not Jewish; they are Bible-believing Christians," Evans told Fox News Digital. "The Christian Zionists worldwide don’t necessarily agree on the politics, but they agree on the people. They are uniting with the people of Israel."

The delegation includes many young people as part of an effort to reach a generation that Evans said had been "poisoned" by countries such as Qatar at universities, as well as by artificial intelligence.

The summit, held in cooperation with Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, opened Tuesday with an event on Jerusalem’s Mount of Olives. Evans said the site, which is associated with Jesus and his ascension, holds particular significance for participants and serves as a symbol of their faith.
Israel’s Special Envoy to the Christian World George Deek said he was proud of the sustained support Israel has received from Jewish and Christian communities abroad since Oct. 7, 2023.
LOST CITY WHERE JESUS PERFORMED MIRACLES HAS FINALLY BEEN IDENTIFIED, EXPERT SAYS

"The arrival of Christian leaders carries a powerful message that Israel does not stand alone. They have come to bear witness, meet people whose lives were shattered on Oct. 7 and carry their stories back to communities around the world," Deek told Fox News Digital.
Deek said the bond between Israel and the Christian world has been built on "truth, courage and sheer determination" to confront antisemitism and other forms of hatred wherever they arise.

"This visit is a testament to the strength of the bond between Israel and Christian communities despite attempts by various groups, including paid actors and anti-Israel organizations, to drive a wedge between them," he added.

Deek said the special relationship between Christians and Jews rests on three foundations: a shared biblical heritage; a commitment to ensuring Jews can live free from antisemitism and fear and the right of Christians in the Middle East and elsewhere to live without intimidation.
Anti-Israel activists hold banners that include, "globalize the intifada" during a protest commemorating Nakba Day May 15, 2025, in Brooklyn, N.Y. (Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty Images)

"The future of the Jews in Israel and the future of Christians are connected because we have a shared history. We share the same historical land, the same values, kings and prophets, and we have to stand together, especially when it comes to this warfare against the soul of Christians, trying to drive them away from Israel," Deek told Fox News Digital.
Influencer Oli London first visited Israel six weeks after the Oct. 7 attack, traveling to Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where residents were killed and kidnapped and homes were burned during the massacre.

"I felt it was so important to come back to honor the memory of the victims, advocate for those still suffering from trauma, raise awareness of their suffering and take part in mass prayers," London told Fox News Digital.
SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

"I think it’s also important to show Christians the holy sites in Israel. I’m visiting the Sea of Galilee, the Mount of Olives, the Garden Tomb and other biblical sites to encourage Christians to return because Israel has had a difficult time over the past few years," he continued.
London also praised the resilience of the Jewish people and addressed rising antisemitism around the world since Oct. 7.

"Sadly, many people are either staying silent or jumping on the bandwagon of the anti-Israel trend, fueling hatred and bringing out antisemitic views in many people. Jewish people need support and need to know they are loved and supported by so many Christians," he said.

A woman reacts as the community of Kibbutz Kfar Aza commemorates members who were killed, taken hostage and who died in captivity, after the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas terrorists, in Kibbutz Kfar Aza, southern Israel, Oct. 16, 2025. (Hannah McKay/Reuters)

On Thursday, members of the delegation will visit the Nova music festival site, where one of the central massacres of Oct. 7 took place, and meet with released hostages Romi Gonen, Elkana Bohbot and Noa Argamani, who were abducted from the festival. On Friday, the delegation will visit the ancient site of Shiloh in Samaria for a special tour and prayer event.

Hooman Khalili, who is participating in the summit, was born in Iran and has been an outspoken supporter of Israel. He said he has visited the country 17 times over 21 months to create "Woman, Life, Freedom" murals.

"I was invited and saw it as an opportunity to share with American pastors the work I have been doing to show the world how Israel and the Jewish people support women and the people of Iran," he told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"This is one of those opportunities to come and pray for the land and the State of Israel, connect with other Christians and people who share my beliefs and values."
Amelie Botbol is a freelance field reporter based in Tel Aviv, Israel, who reports on Israel-related news.

title: Mike Waltz fights back tears revealing what Hamas hostage refused to do before release
summary: Eliya Cohen, freed after 505 days in Hamas captivity, and Nova festival survivor Ziv Abud shared their harrowing stories at the United Nations.
story: Eliya Cohen and Nova survivor Ziv Abud recount the Hamas attack and captivity as U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz vows America will continue to stand with Israel.

UNITED NATIONS — Three years after the worst massacre in Israel’s history, Eliya Cohen — who survived 505 days in Hamas captivity — took the stage at the United Nations alongside his newlywed wife, Ziv Abud, a survivor of the Nova music festival massacre, and tried to explain to some of the world’s top diplomats what he had endured.

"They didn't let me change clothes or to get a shower, even to eat or to drink," he said. "They chained me with heavy iron chains by my leg," Cohen said during an emotional discussion moderated by Dr. Phil McGraw at Israel’s U.N. commemoration Tuesday.

He said lights were kept on to prevent the hostages from sleeping and that captors would enter repeatedly during the night screaming in an effort to frighten them. Cohen said they were not permitted to use a restroom and that at times survival felt almost impossible.
FREED HOSTAGE ROM BRASLAVSKI DETAILS ABUSE, STARVATION DURING 738 DAYS IN GAZA CAPTIVITY

U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz, Israeli Ambassador Danny Danon, freed hostage Eliya Cohen, Nova massacre survivor Ziv Abud, Israeli military observer Oriya Berlin, Dr. Phil McGraw, FOX Business anchor Liz Claman and Israeli musician Idan Raichel gather at U.N. headquarters in New York for Israel’s Oct. 7 commemoration, Oct. 6, 2026. (Israeli Mission to the UN)
But he described repeatedly forcing his mind away from the violence and toward the possibility of returning home.

"Don't think about the violence. Don't think about the torture. Don't think about everything," Cohen recalled telling himself. "Just continue, stay strong. And maybe one day, you will come back home to your family."

Cohen was among the 251 people abducted during the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack, when about 1,200 people were killed in southern Israel in their homes and at the Nova Music festival. It was the deadliest single day in Israel’s history. He personally lost 48 people he knew that day.
His wife, Ziv, carried a different piece of the same story.

Abud and Cohen had arrived at the Nova festival shortly before dawn with her 19-year-old nephew Amit and his girlfriend Karin. When the attack began, they eventually took refuge in a roadside bomb shelter that Cohen said was designed for roughly eight people but became packed with 29.
HAMAS USED SEXUAL VIOLENCE 'DELIBERATELY AND SYSTEMATICALLY' ON OCT 7, COMMISSION REPORT FINDS

Eliya Cohen, who was kidnapped during the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attack, gestures as a crowd welcomes him while he arrives home from hospital, in Tzur Hadassah, Israel, March 4, 2025. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)

Abud told the audience that more than 40 terrorists later attacked the shelter with grenades and gunfire. One man inside repeatedly grabbed grenades and threw them back outside before he was killed, she said.
As the attack continued, Cohen covered Abud with bodies — an act that saved her life.
"I lost my consciousness. Eliya was kidnapped," Abud said. "And after seven hours, I woke up in the shelter. I found myself in a pile of bodies."
She paused, fighting back the tears. "It wasn't even bodies. It was body parts."
Abud said she then saw that Amit and Karin had been killed. "I needed to sit with the bodies for seven more hours," she said. She was eventually rescued, one of seven survivors from the shelter.
"We were four people that went to the festival from the same house," Abud said, "And I'm the only one that came back home that night."
FORMER HAMAS HOSTAGE COUNTERS HASAN PIKER’S UT AUSTIN EVENT WITH HER STORY OF SURVIVAL
This screengrab from a video released on Aug. 1, 2025, by Hamas, shows Israeli hostage Evyatar David looking weak and malnourished. (AFP via Getty Images)
For 505 days, she campaigned for Cohen’s return without knowing whether the man she loved would ever come home. Cohen, meanwhile, said he believed while in captivity that Abud had been killed.
The couple married weeks before Tuesday’s ceremony.
"But now he's here," Abud said. "And I can look forward to the future after we got married."
She said she hoped the years ahead would include "kids and family because we are here and we survived. And we need to live a normal life," she said.
Another Oct. 7 survivor who addressed the diplomats was Oriya Berlin, a young Israeli visual intelligence observer who had arrived at a base in the Gaza border area just two days before the attack.
Berlin said she woke on the morning of Oct. 7 believing she was hearing a thunderstorm.
"Outside, thousands of missiles were raining down with a single objective: to destroy my life and the lives of my friends," she said.

Berlin and four other soldiers ran barefoot and in pajamas into a small shelter. They were unarmed. She said the women initially believed the incursion would resemble scenarios they had studied during training — a small squad that Israeli forces could quickly contain.

Seconds later, she said, they heard vehicles and gunfire. Berlin described roughly 60 heavily armed terrorists attacking the base. At one point, she said, a message appeared in the unit’s WhatsApp group telling soldiers to shout "IDF" in Hebrew so Israeli troops could find them. The broken Hebrew immediately raised suspicions that a terrorist had taken a soldier’s phone.
They remained silent.
Berlin said they then heard another group shouting for soldiers to identify themselves, followed by a burst of gunfire and silence.
Ten hours after the attack began, she said, special forces finally reached them.
THE SENATE HAS REMEMBERED AMERICA’S OCTOBER 7TH VICTIMS. NOW IT’S TIME TO HEAL
Memorials at the site of the Oct. 7 Hamas terror attack on the Supernova music festival near Kibbutz Re'im, Israel, on May 27, 2024. (Kobi Wolf/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Berlin said that after learning how many of her friends had been murdered or kidnapped, she could not remain at home. Although she was offered the opportunity to leave military service, Berlin said she refused and returned as an observer for another six months before later moving into the IDF Public Diplomacy Office.

"I wanted the world to see that the IDF is not just an intimidating military force on a television screen," she said. "It was also a 5'2" fake blonde girl like me who simply wanted to protect her home, her family, and her friends."

She said she has since spoken before audiences ranging from international organizations to high school students who told her "I was wasting their time because of their deep-seated anti-Israel hostility." "But I stayed," Berlin said. "I spoke because the truth demands a voice."
Berlin said her decision to continue speaking was rooted in the friends who did not survive.

Before the ceremony, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz met privately with Cohen and Abud, asking Cohen how he was feeling physically and telling the couple how good it was to see them "healthy and alive."
Minutes later, from the stage, Waltz became visibly emotional as he recounted a part of Cohen’s captivity that he said he had been unable to get out of his mind.
Waltz said that on the night before Cohen’s release, Hamas tried to make him record a propaganda video claiming he had been treated well. "He refused," Waltz said. "He held firm. He said no."
Waltz said Hamas again tried to turn Cohen’s release into propaganda the following day, placing him before cameras and instructing him to raise his hands.
"He refused again," Waltz said. "Eliya, we salute you. I salute you," Waltz continued. "You are a proud, strong Jew. You're undefeated, man" he said with his voice breaking.

The hostage crisis stretched over two years and several rounds of negotiations, releases and rescue operations. Waltz told Fox News Digital after Tuesday’s ceremony that he wanted the commemoration to acknowledge both the loss of Oct. 7 and how much had changed since.
"Oct. 7, 2023, was their 9/11, was their Pearl Harbor," Waltz said. "More Jews were brutally massacred that day than any day since the Holocaust."
ISRAELI OCTOBER 7 SURVIVORS CONQUER TRAUMA ALONGSIDE LEGENDARY ROCK ICONS IN POWERFUL NEW DOCUMENTARY
Protesters rallied near the United Nations, demanding immediate medical care and release of hostages held by Hamas. (Yoav Ginsburg/Hostages and Missing Families Forum)
He said it was important "to recognize the loss" and "hear directly from the survivors," but also to take stock of the region three years later.

"We have President Trump's 20-point peace plan. We have a U.N. resolution establishing the International Stabilization Force," Waltz told Fox News Digital. "He's determined to not repeat what's happened so often in the past, where Hamas rebuilds, Iran rearms, they attack again, and you have this devastation all over again."
Waltz pointed to broader shifts across the Middle East.
"Iran is on its back foot. Lebanon has hope, Syria has hope. Iraq has hope," he said.
He said he hoped the commemoration could combine "remembrance, the perspective, and I think charting, trying to chart a path of hope and peace for the future."

From the stage, Waltz argued that Oct. 7 had produced the opposite strategic result from what Iran and its allies sought. "Oct. 7 completely, and I think irreversibly, has backfired on Iran and all of their terrorist proxies," he said, pointing to changes in Syria, Lebanon and Iraq and the expansion of Israel’s regional relationships.
He ended with a message to the audience: "America will stand with the Jewish people."

"Be strong. Be resilient. Be wise," Waltz said. "And know that what you're doing is right. Stand with your moral compass and know that this administration, the United States of America, stands with you."
Israeli Ambassador to the U.N. Danny Danon used the gathering — attended by ambassadors and diplomats from multiple countries — to turn his attention to the institution hosting it.
MOTHER OF OCTOBER 7 HOSTAGE WHO WAS EXECUTED UNPACKS HER GRIEF IN NEW MEMOIR
Israeli Ambassador Danny Danon and U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz attend Israel’s Oct. 7 commemoration at U.N. headquarters in New York, Oct. 6, 2026. (Israeli mission to the UN)
"Even in this building, the U.N. is trying to demonize and isolate Israel," Danon said. "They have turned the victim into the accused, comparing our IDF soldiers to Hamas terrorists."
Danon said he has been told by colleagues that he takes criticism of Israel at the U.N. ‘too personally’.

"Indeed, it is personal," he responded. "My daughter is serving right now in the IDF. My son served as an officer in the IDF," Danon said. "He was supposed to be on the Re'im base next to Gaza on Oct. 7. The last minute, he was released home for the holiday."

"That's why it's personal," Danon said. "The U.N. tries to demonize all of our sons and daughters, our lions and lionesses who give everything so we can freely live in our homeland. So yes, it is personal. It's personal for all of us."
For Cohen and Abud, however, the event eventually returned from geopolitics to something much smaller: the possibility of an ordinary future.
Abud said they hoped to have children and build a family despite knowing that Oct. 7 and the 505 days that followed would remain part of their lives.
Cohen, asked by McGraw what he would say if the terrorists who abducted and tortured him were watching, needed only a few words.
"I won," Cohen said.
"I won and I'm here."
He then turned his message outward.

Freed Israeli hostage Eliya Cohen and his wife, Nova massacre survivor Ziv Abud, speak with Dr. Phil McGraw during Israel’s Oct. 7 commemoration at U.N. headquarters in New York, Oct. 6, 2026. (Israeli mission to the UN)
"Stay proud to be Jewish," Cohen said. "And stay proud to be Israeli."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We are here to stay."

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Former CIA officer warns against trusting Russia's account of mysterious death in Siberia
summary: Glenn Corn, a former CIA officer, explains why Vladimir Putin's Kremlin cannot be trusted on the Russian researcher's death, citing past coverups.
story: Glenn Corn, who spent over 20 years in U.S. intelligence, says Russia's history of deception warrants skepticism as questions remain over the pneumonia death of a 28-year-old researcher who worked at a lab with deadly pathogens.

Glenn Corn, a former CIA officer, told Fox News Digital that Russia’s decades-long history of deception makes it difficult to trust the Kremlin’s account of a possible disease outbreak following the death of a 28-year-old researcher at a facility containing dangerous pathogens.
Darya Shipilova, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, got sick near the end of September.

After unconfirmed reports that Shipilova died from pneumonic plague were shared far and wide on social media, Russian authorities pushed back, saying she died on Oct. 2 from "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing found no evidence she had been infected with a pathogen from her lab.
Yet the Russian government’s past messaging around major crises has left Corn and others wary of its official account.
Glenn Corn attends a discussion organized by the Kyiv Security Forum in Kyiv, Ukraine, on April 3, 2026. (Yuliia Ovsiannikova/Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)
RUSSIAN RESEARCHER'S MYSTERY DEATH COULD BE ‘FAR WORSE’ THAN THE PLAGUE, FORMER SENIOR TRUMP OFFICIAL WARNS

"This is what the challenge is, because they have the history of the 'boy who cried wolf syndrome.' They have this history of being deceitful. It's very hard to believe what they're saying," said Corn, a professor at the Institute of World Politics, a graduate school in Washington, D.C.

Corn, who is fluent in Russian and spent more than 20 years overseas during his intelligence career, gave several examples of elaborate Russian coverups, including the 1979 anthrax outbreak that killed at least 64 people in the Soviet city of Sverdlovsk, now called Yekaterinburg.

For years, the Soviet Union claimed that the deaths were caused by intestinal anthrax from tainted meat, according to PBS' "Frontline." It wasn't until 1992 that President Boris Yeltsin finally admitted the illnesses were the result of military activity at a nearby biological weapons facility.
This dedication to deception, Corn said, remains a feature of the current government under President Vladimir Putin.

Darya Shipilova, 28, an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died after developing pneumonia of an unknown cause, prompting quarantines and heightened health precautions in the region. Russian authorities say testing has found no evidence her illness was linked to pathogens she worked with. (East2West news)
AMB. GORDON SONDLAND: THE GODFATHER TEST -- HOW PUTIN TURNS EVERY ATTACK INTO A MYSTERY—AND GETS AWAY WITH IT

Corn pointed to the Kremlin’s past denials of ties to the Wagner mercenary group, whose murky relationship with the state allowed its fighters to advance Moscow’s interests overseas while Russian officials maintained plausible deniability. Putin later acknowledged that the group had been fully financed by the Russian state.

"This goes to the strategic culture of leadership in Russia... and their fear of the rest of the world, and their belief that they have to deceive everybody because everybody is deceiving them," Corn said.

Corn said this style of narrative control is also characteristic of China, which remains under Communist Party rule, while modern Russia inherited many of the institutions and governing practices of the communist-led Soviet Union.

For example, China faced criticism in the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic for withholding or delaying the release of critical information about the emerging virus, which has gone on to kill more than 7 million people globally.
Workers in protective uniforms conduct testing in Russia amid heightened precautions following the death of an employee at a Siberian anti-plague research institute. (Khuvsguliinungu.mn/e2w)
TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR

"In both systems, people are disincentivized to tell the truth when there's a bad story," Corn said. "Nobody wants to actually say that we have a real problem and we need to deal with it because they're afraid that it will cost them their jobs, their lives, their freedom."

With that history in mind, Corn said U.S. officials should not simply take Moscow at its word on Shipilova’s death, but independently verify its claims and closely monitor for any signs of a wider outbreak.

So far, there is no sign that Shipilova’s illness has spread. Russia's health watchdog said Tuesday that 60% of the roughly 200 people quarantined after potentially coming in contact with Shipilova have been released. It added that no cases of plague have been found.
Russia's President Vladimir Putin chairs a Security Council meeting via videolink in Moscow on Oct. 7, 2026. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The World Health Organization (WHO) said Tuesday that the case presented a "very low" risk outside Russia, The Associated Press reported.

That same day, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on social media that the global health agency is in contact with Russian health authorities and has requested more information "to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia" that killed Shipilova.
President Donald Trump also told reporters on Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Putin about the case "very soon," adding that the U.S. is already in "very deep discussions" with Russia.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Federal judge orders pro-Trump TV ads funded by taxpayers off air immediately
summary: In an earlier filing, the administration said it had planned to stop ad purchases Sunday.
story: A federal judge ordered the Trump administration on Sunday to stop airing ads funded by the U.S. government that portray President Donald Trump in a favorable light, effective immediately.

The lawsuit was brought by the watchdog group Common Cause; Robert Hunter, a Democratic candidate for a seat in the Alabama state House; and a labor union in New York and its political action committee. The suit was one of several similar complaints — including one by the Democratic National Committee — that were filed to get the ads off the air.

“Plaintiffs have demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest,” U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon of the Southern District of New York wrote.

The administration had said in a court filing Saturday that the Department of Homeland Security, via a vendor, had placed ad buys through Sunday and had told the vendor to not purchase ads beyond that day.

Rochon said the plaintiffs’ argument was not moot, however, and ordered the Trump administration to “cancel or cause to be cancelled” any ads from airing or being disseminated, including those set to air Sunday night.
Rochon also wrote that the administration was barred from using funds appropriated to DHS to “develop, create, disseminate, place, distribute, publish, or air the challenged advertisements.”

The White House, DHS and the Office of Management and Budget, which are all named as defendants in the suit, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the ruling. MAGA Inc., which Trump had said last week would help him fund the ads moving forward, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
For Subscribers

“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs said in a statement. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”
For Subscribers
Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón said that despite the ruling, “our fight continues.”
“We won’t stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again,” Solomón said.
The ads — one of which was nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad — came under scrutiny by critics who argued that using taxpayer money could be illegal and called the spots propaganda.

title: South Carolina Senate rivals spar over Iran, AI and Trump in debate
summary: Annie Andrews and Darline Graham are running to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, and the winner will make history as the first female senator elected from South Carolina.
story: Republican Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews clashed Sunday night in their first and perhaps only debate of the general election, tangling over President Donald Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill,” the high costs of gas and goods, the Iran war and AI data centers.

South Carolina is a ruby-red state where Trump remains popular among Republican voters. But the race has tightened in the closing stretch of the campaign, and Democrats believe they have a shot at knocking off Graham, who was appointed to fill her brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat after his sudden death in July. The top Senate Republican super PAC has pledged to spend $5 million to shore up Graham’s campaign.
At the start of the debate, hosted in Columbia by South Carolina ETV, Darline Graham noted that Sunday night marked exactly three months since her brother unexpectedly died at age 71.

Andrews, a pediatrician, sought to portray Graham, who previously led a state agency, as an inexperienced empty suit who refuses to stand up to Trump or his unpopular policies. She mocked Graham as “the White House’s ambassador to South Carolina.”

Graham attacked Andrews as the “most radical liberal” to run in South Carolina and as sympathetic to the Democratic Socialist Party. “Annie Andrews will not stand up to the Socialist Democratic Party; she’s only going to join them,” Graham said — a characterization Andrews rejected.

Graham has “been told to come out here and call me Bernie, Ocasio, Mamdani — that’s what’s in her script. But the truth is my name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that,” Andrews said. “The truth is I support the Second Amendment, I believe we need a secure border, and we need to deport illegal immigrants who break the law. ... The real difference between me and Sen. Graham is that I will stand up to my own party, and I will always put South Carolina first.”

Graham and Andrews are running for a full six-year Senate term; the winner will make history as the first female senator elected from South Carolina. The debate also featured Libertarian Kasie Whitener.
For Subscribers

Graham and Andrews tussled over issue after issue. As the country faces Social Security insolvency, Andrews said she would raise caps to make wealthier people pay more but would not hike the retirement age. She added that Republicans like Graham want to privatize Social Security so “Washington insiders” can profit. “Unfortunately, my opponent is in the race to do what Washington insiders tell her,” she said.

Graham shot back that she understands what people in her state are facing. When her parents died at a young age, Social Security benefits helped her and her brother survive. Graham said Andrews’ criticism of Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill” is misplaced because it lowered taxes on tips and Social Security. “You called it the one big, ugly bill, so here you are deceiving the people of South Carolina,” Graham said.

On affordability, Graham said she has “lived paycheck to paycheck” before and acknowledged that “gas prices are high right now. ... I feel the pain, too.” She said that she supports suspending the gas tax and that easing regulations on drilling would permanently bring prices down.
Andrews pinned blame for high gas prices on Graham, who she said voted several times against a war powers resolution to restrict Trump’s war with Iran.
For Subscribers

“The war is the exact reason we now have record-high gas and diesel prices. Farmers are getting crushed, and everything costs more,” Andrews said. “My opponent is the only one who had the opportunity to vote to end the war, but three times in a row she voted to continue it.”

Andrews also dinged Graham for admitting during a previous debate that “national security is not my thing.” “South Carolina, if your surgeon said that appendectomies aren’t really his thing, would you still hand him a scalpel? No,” Andrews said. “So why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the U.S. Senate? She is unserious and unqualified.”
Graham retorted that she wants the war to end, like everyone does, but said she believes in “peace through strength.” Then, she went after Andrews over the national security quip.

“But talking about not my thing, let’s talk about what’s not your thing. Your thing apparently is not being honest with the people of South Carolina. At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight,” Graham said without getting specific. “But you have, you are deceiving the people of South Carolina. You have flip-flopped on everything. There’s so many social media posts out there to prove it. Shame on you!”
The proliferation of data centers, which power artificial intelligence companies, has become a major flash point in the midterm elections.

Andrews went right after Graham on the issue, nicknaming her “Data Center Darline.” Andrews said her data-center plan calls for a “two-year moratorium, protections to ensure your rates don’t go up and a return to real local control.”

Graham fired back that stopping construction of all data centers would allow China to win the race for AI dominance. She said she voted for the Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to shift higher energy costs from building data centers from consumers onto AI companies.

“Under her Bernie Sanders plan, a two-year moratorium, that is dangerous to the national security of our country, because in two years China is going to be so far ahead [that] we are going to be in so much trouble,” Graham said, adding that local communities should decide whether data centers get built in their backyards.
“I want communities to decide. She wants the federal government to decide.”

title: The Commanders had seconds left to secure a win — and blew it
summary: The Washington Commanders were on their way to beating the New York Giants in overtime. Then they ran out the clock on themselves and settled for a tie.
story: When the snap that left the entire NFL in disbelief began Sunday, Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels was supposed to do one of two things, Commanders coach Dan Quinn said — throw the ball out of bounds or spike it into the turf.
Both would have stopped the clock and given Washington the chance to earn a season-reviving win in the final seconds of overtime over their division-leading rival, the New York Giants.
When Daniels did neither, however, and instead ran the ball, it set off a chain of events that produced a 27-27 tie that was the result of the most inexplicable ending of the young NFL season so far.
“Leaving tonight with a tie feels like a loss,” Quinn said.
It was a far cry from the optimism the day had started with for Washington.

Playing for the first time since he injured an elbow three weeks earlier, Daniels had at times resembled the player who took the NFL by storm as a rookie in 2024. His 38-yard touchdown run in the third quarter gave Washington a 19-6 lead. In the fourth quarter, another Daniels touchdown run of 26 yards kept his team in front, 27-13, with 11 minutes to play in regulation.
The Commanders had just seven more offensive plays the rest of the fourth quarter, while the Giants roared back for two touchdowns to force overtime, with the teams lodged in a 27-all tie.
And still, the Commanders had the opportunity to win.

With 13 seconds left in overtime, the Commanders were in range of a game-winning field goal, just 26 yards from the end zone. Daniels, feeling some defensive pressure, improvised a run and barely got back to the line of scrimmage with 8 seconds left on the clock. He lay on the turf nonchalantly for 2 more seconds, until the Commanders seemed to remember they did not have a timeout left and that the clock was running out on their opportunity to win the game.
“They don’t have a timeout,” Fox broadcaster Chris Myers said. “What are they doing?”

Players from both teams scrambled into position, blocking the official from spotting the ball until no time was left on the clock. Myers, on the Fox broadcast, recalled the chaotic final sequence as a “comedy of errors.” Quinn threw his headset to the ground in frustration.
“I was surprised,” Giants coach John Harbaugh said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The 27-27 tie was officially over. But the explanations had just begun.
Daniels called out the need to play better “situational football” and blamed himself.
“We got to stop the clock,” Daniels said afterward. “It starts from everybody top down, but ultimately, you know, it’s on me.”
Quinn said to blame him, the coach.

“The sequencing of that does not fall on him,” Quinn said. “It’s an outside throw or a clock [spike],” Quinn said. “Those are the two: out-of-bounds throw or a clock, and it has to come from me. I don’t have to put him into that spot. I can do that earlier, and we can finish the kick earlier. We don’t need to gain more yards, so that’s on me.”
Why not just spike the ball with 13 seconds left instead of have Daniels drop back at all?
“I’m saying we don’t need to gain any more” yards to make the field goal shorter, Quinn said. “We’re just trying to gain more. We don’t need to.”

Commanders minority owner Magic Johnson posted on X that he was “in total disbelief my Commanders had such poor clock management in today’s overtime game against the Giants. All we had to do was kick the field goal and we would have won the game! 🤦🏾‍♂️”

Quinn’s desire to run a play and either gain a few more yards or drain a few more seconds of clock was perhaps rooted in what had taken place during a pair of wild finishes earlier this season that had shown the perils of leaving too much time on the clock.

Only hours earlier Sunday, the Philadelphia Eagles kicked a go-ahead field goal to take the lead on Jacksonville with just 8 seconds left in regulation. But that was enough time for the Jaguars to run the ensuing kickoff back into range for what became a game-winning field goal to stun the Eagles. Two weeks ago, Baltimore trailed when it got the ball back with only 7 seconds left in regulation but was able to move into field-goal range for a game-winning kick to beat Dallas.

Both of the wild endings produced by the Jaguars and the Ravens required huge, yard-gaining plays. All the Commanders needed to secure their own win was a spike, one of the simplest plays in football.
“I’m gutted for our team,” Quinn said. “And that’s the hardest part.”

title: The 49ers look like the NFL’s best team after surviving a heavyweight fight
summary: Behind quarterback Brock Purdy, the San Francisco 49ers beat the Seattle Seahawks on the road — and appear to be the NFL’s best team through five weeks.
story: The last time San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy played in Seattle, he could lead an injury-laden 49ers team to only two field goals in a 35-point playoff loss to the Super Bowl-bound Seahawks.
On Sunday, Purdy led San Francisco to a game-winning drive in the fourth quarter of a 32-29 win, handing Seattle its first home loss in 371 days.

Is San Francisco headed to the Super Bowl next? There’s a long way to go, but the 49ers are 5-0 for the third time under coach Kyle Shanahan — and the last two times they were still playing in February.

Sunday’s game was an instant classic, a matchup filled with wild moments and playoff intensity. The teams combined for a whopping seven turnovers and multiple personal fouls, and one player — San Francisco linebacker Dre Greenlaw — was even ejected.
The defenses largely dominated until the fourth quarter. That was when Purdy, perhaps the MVP favorite through the first four weeks and change of the NFL season, stepped up.

Trailing 26-21, Purdy led the 49ers on a 12-play, 74-yard touchdown drive that culminated in a 7-yard touchdown pass to Mike Evans. Purdy then threw to Evans again to convert a 2-point attempt to put San Francisco ahead 29-26.
After a Seattle field goal, the 49ers traveled 43 yards in eight plays for a 44-yard field goal that proved to be the game winner.

“I thought Brock did an unbelievable job finding a way there to win at the end,” Shanahan said. “There were some ups and downs. By no means was everything perfect. He was really good in the fourth quarter.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
On the Seahawks’ final possession, the offense couldn’t convert a fourth-and-10 — though whether receiver Cooper Kupp was able to stretch the ball for a first down on the play seemed up for debate.

While neither quarterback was great Sunday, Purdy had some impressive moments considering the circumstances. Facing the NFL’s second-best defense in expected points added per play, Purdy capitalized on early turnovers before he managed the two scoring drives in the fourth.
And he did so with a depleted receiving corps. The 49ers entered Sunday with four receivers on injured reserve. Then Deebo Samuel and Jacob Cowing were injured during the game.

“We got a bunch of warriors,” Shanahan said of the backups who stepped up. “Everyone knows the talent and the stars of some of the guys on our team. What makes our guys special is how much they love football, how much they give it up every week.”
Among those who played key roles Sunday was Evans, who caught a season-high seven passes for 113 yards and a score, plus the 2-pointer for good measure.
“He’s a game-changer,” Purdy said. “As a quarterback, any time I have to go to him it always feels good.”
Evans told Fox after the game: “We knew it was going to be a dogfight. They’re a great team, and we came out here and showed we’re a great team, as well.”

Purdy finished with a so-so stat line by his standards: 19 of 29 passing for 189 yards, two touchdowns and one interception. More important, though, he outplayed his counterpart, Sam Darnold, and found a way to shepherd two go-ahead drives in the game’s biggest moments.
